paper.title: One week of sleep restriction raises fasting glucose: primary and subgroup results

paper_doc.running_head: J. Fake Metabolism 2021; 9: 211-226 · doi:10.9999/fake.2021.016 · Original article
paper_doc.title: One week of sleep restriction raises fasting glucose: primary and subgroup results
paper_doc.authors: Lindqvist, E.¹, Abara, N.²  ¹ Department of Clinical Physiology, Fake University Hospital; ² Institute of Nutrition and Metabolism, Fake Northern University. Correspondence: E. Lindqvist. Received 3 August 2020; accepted 19 January 2021.
paper_doc.abstract: Background: Short habitual sleep is associated with type 2 diabetes in cohort studies, but experimental evidence comes mostly from small laboratory studies of a few nights. Methods: In a randomised two-period crossover trial, 90 healthy adults spent one week with time in bed restricted to 5 hours a night and one week with habitual time in bed of 8.5 hours, at home, separated by a washout of at least three weeks. Adherence was monitored by wrist actigraphy. The primary outcome was fasting plasma glucose on the morning after the seventh night of each condition; a subgroup analysis by body mass index was prespecified. Results: Actigraphy confirmed a large difference in sleep between the conditions, and fasting glucose was higher after the restricted week. The primary analysis and the prespecified subgroup analysis are reported in full in the Results. Conclusions: One week of restricted sleep at home raises fasting glucose in healthy adults. Sleep should be considered in the interpretation of fasting glucose measurements and in diabetes prevention research.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Adults in many countries sleep less than the seven or more hours a night recommended for health, and the share of working adults who report short sleep on work days has grown over the past three decades [1]. Short habitual sleep is associated in prospective cohort studies with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, independent of body weight and physical activity as far as these can be measured [2, 3]. Associations of this kind are, however, open to confounding by shift work, depression, low income, chronic pain and other factors that both shorten sleep and worsen metabolic health, so they cannot by themselves show that sleep loss raises blood glucose [4].
Experimental studies offer a more direct test. Laboratory studies that restricted sleep for a few nights have reported reduced insulin sensitivity measured by intravenous glucose tolerance tests or hyperinsulinaemic clamps [5-7]. Most of these studies enrolled fewer than twenty young men, held participants in a sleep laboratory under conditions of controlled light, food and activity that differ from daily life, and measured outcomes after two to five nights [8]. Whether a longer period of restriction at home, of the kind many working adults experience during a busy week, changes fasting glucose in a broader sample of adults is less clear [9, 10].
Fasting glucose is a simple, cheap and widely measured outcome that clinicians already use to screen for impaired glucose regulation and to diagnose diabetes. A change in fasting glucose that persists over a week of short sleep would be relevant to the interpretation of routine blood tests, which are usually taken without any record of recent sleep, and to advice on sleep as part of diabetes prevention [11].
There are also reasons to expect that the response to sleep loss might differ between people. Adiposity is linked to lower insulin sensitivity at baseline, and people with obesity may have less reserve with which to compensate for a further metabolic stress [12, 13]. Sex, age and habitual sleep duration have also been proposed as modifiers of the metabolic response to sleep loss, although the evidence for each is limited [14].
We therefore conducted a randomised crossover trial in healthy adults, comparing one week of restricted time in bed at home with one week of habitual sleep. The primary outcome was fasting plasma glucose at the end of each week. A prespecified secondary analysis examined whether the effect differed by body mass index (BMI).

sections.heading: 2. Methods
sections.text: The trial was conducted at the clinical research unit of Fake University Hospital. The protocol, including the primary outcome, the analysis model and the subgroup analysis by BMI, was registered before the first participant was enrolled (registry number FAKE-2018-0412), and is available from the corresponding author. The report follows the extension of the CONSORT statement for randomised crossover trials.

sections.heading: 2.1 Participants
sections.text:
We recruited adults aged 20 to 55 years through advertisements at two university campuses, in local community centres and on a regional health website between March 2018 and October 2019. Eligible participants reported habitual sleep of seven to nine hours a night on work days, had a regular daytime schedule, and were free of diagnosed diabetes, cardiovascular disease, sleep disorders and psychiatric illness.
We excluded people who worked night or rotating shifts, had travelled across more than two time zones in the previous month, used medication known to affect glucose metabolism or sleep, were pregnant or breastfeeding, or scored above 10 on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale. People who reported loud habitual snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing were referred for clinical assessment and not enrolled.
Screening included a clinical interview, a questionnaire on sleep habits and chronotype, measurement of height, weight and blood pressure, and one week of wrist actigraphy to confirm habitual sleep timing. All participants gave written informed consent and received a fixed payment for each completed study week. The study was approved by the regional ethics committee (approval 2017/1189).

sections.heading: 2.2 Design and sleep conditions
sections.text:
The trial used a randomised two-period crossover design. Each participant completed one week of habitual sleep, with time in bed set to 8.5 hours a night, and one week of restricted sleep, with time in bed set to 5 hours a night. The order of the two weeks was assigned by a computer-generated sequence in blocks of four, prepared by a statistician who had no contact with participants, and concealed in numbered opaque envelopes until the end of screening. The two weeks were separated by a washout of at least three weeks of unrestricted sleep.
During the restricted week, participants kept their usual wake time and delayed their bedtime, so that the timing of morning light exposure, work and meals remained close to their routine. Participants slept at home throughout. Adherence was monitored with a wrist actigraph worn continuously on the non-dominant arm and with a daily sleep diary, and study staff sent a text-message reminder half an hour before the scheduled bedtime on each night.
Participants were asked not to nap, to keep caffeine intake at their usual level and to take none after 14:00, and to avoid alcohol throughout both weeks. Physical activity was not prescribed but was recorded by the same actigraph as daily step counts.

sections.heading: 2.3 Diet
sections.text: Because changes in food intake could mediate or mask effects of sleep loss on glucose, participants were asked to keep their usual diet in both weeks and completed a three-day food record, covering two work days and one free day, in each week. Records were coded by a dietitian who was unaware of the condition. On the evening before each outcome visit, participants ate a standardised meal provided by the study, finished by 20:00, and then fasted, apart from water, until the visit.

sections.heading: 2.4 Outcome measures
sections.text:
Outcome visits took place on the morning after the seventh night of each condition, between 07:30 and 09:00. A trained research nurse drew venous blood after the participant had rested seated for 15 minutes. Plasma was separated within 30 minutes and stored at -80 °C. Glucose was measured by a hexokinase method in a single accredited laboratory, in batches that contained samples from both conditions, by staff who were unaware of the condition.
Secondary outcomes were fasting insulin, subjective sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, rated each morning on waking and at the outcome visit, and mood on a brief visual analogue scale. Height and weight were measured at the screening visit with the participant in light clothing and without shoes, and BMI was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres. Actigraphic sleep was scored with the manufacturer's validated algorithm, using the sleep diary to set the rest interval for each night.

sections.heading: 2.5 Statistical analysis
sections.text:
The sample size was chosen to give 90% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 to detect a difference in fasting glucose that earlier laboratory studies suggested was plausible, with an allowance for 15% attrition.
The primary analysis used a linear mixed model with condition, period and sequence as fixed effects and participant as a random effect, and included all participants who completed both periods. We checked for carry-over by testing the sequence-by-condition interaction, and for a period effect by the period term. Secondary outcomes were analysed with the same model; morning sleepiness ratings across the week were analysed with a further term for day.
The subgroup analysis by BMI was prespecified in the registered protocol. It added to the primary model a term for BMI category (30 or below, above 30) and its interaction with condition. Missing food records were not imputed. Analyses were done in R version 3.6 with the lme4 package. We report estimates with 95% confidence intervals throughout.

sections.heading: 3.1 Participants and adherence
sections.text: Of 214 people screened, 104 were randomised and 90 completed both periods and were included in the analysis (Figure 1). The main reasons for withdrawal after randomisation were changes in work schedule, illness unrelated to the study and loss of interest. Table 1 shows the characteristics of the participants at screening. No serious adverse events occurred; two participants reported a minor fall during the restricted week, neither of which needed medical care.

rows: Habitual sleep on work days, h, mean (SD)

sections.text: Actigraphy confirmed that the conditions differed as intended. Mean actigraphic sleep was 7.4 hours a night in the habitual week and 4.7 hours in the restricted week (Figure 2). Most participants kept within 30 minutes of the scheduled bedtime on at least six of the seven nights, and diaries and actigraphy agreed closely on bedtimes. Daily step counts and energy intake from the food records did not differ meaningfully between the two weeks.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Actigraphic sleep duration on each night of the habitual and restricted weeks (mean and 95% confidence interval).

sections.heading: 3.2 Primary outcome
sections.text:
Table 2 gives the primary analysis: fasting glucose rose by 0.4 mmol/L (95% CI 0.2 to 0.6).
There was no evidence of carry-over between periods and no period effect. Individual values at the end of each week are shown in Figure 3.

table.caption: Table 2. Primary analysis: change in fasting plasma glucose after one week of restricted sleep compared with one week of habitual sleep (n = 90).

figure.caption: Figure 3. Individual fasting glucose values at the end of the habitual and restricted weeks; lines join the two values for each participant.

sections.heading: 3.3 Secondary outcomes
sections.text: Sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale was higher at the outcome visit after the restricted week than after the habitual week (difference 1.8 points, 95% CI 1.3 to 2.3), and morning sleepiness rose over the first three days of restriction and then levelled off. Mood ratings were lower during the restricted week (Figure 4). Fasting insulin is reported in the supplementary material.

figure.caption: Figure 4. Morning sleepiness (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale) and mood ratings on each day of the habitual and restricted weeks.

sections.heading: 3.4 Subgroup analysis by BMI
sections.text:
Figure 5 gives the subgroup analysis for participants with BMI above 30: a rise of 0.8 mmol/L.
The estimate for each BMI category is shown with its confidence interval in the same figure.

figure.caption: Figure 5. Change in fasting plasma glucose with restricted sleep, by BMI category (30 or below, above 30), with 95% confidence intervals.

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
In this randomised crossover trial, one week of restricted time in bed at home raised fasting plasma glucose in healthy adults compared with a week of habitual sleep. The trial adds to laboratory studies of a few nights of restriction by showing a change in a routine clinical measure under conditions closer to everyday life, over a full week, and in a sample that included women and a range of ages and body sizes [5-8].
Several mechanisms could link short sleep to higher fasting glucose. Sleep loss increases sympathetic nervous activity and evening cortisol concentrations, both of which promote glucose output by the liver overnight [15, 16]. It also alters the timing of eating and may shorten the overnight fast, although the standardised evening meal before each visit was intended to limit that pathway in our study [17]. Changes in growth hormone secretion and in low-grade inflammation have also been described after restricted sleep, and may contribute [18].
The subgroup analysis by BMI was prespecified and based on a plausible mechanism, but subgroup analyses in trials have limited power and are prone to chance findings, and such results should be read alongside the primary analysis rather than in place of it [19, 20].

sections.heading: 4.1 Strengths and limitations
sections.text:
Strengths of the study include the randomised crossover design, which removes stable differences between participants from the comparison; the objective monitoring of adherence by actigraphy; the standardised timing of blood sampling after a standardised evening meal; and laboratory and dietetic staff who were unaware of the condition. Because participants slept at home and kept their usual wake times, the restriction resembled the short sleep that many adults experience during a working week.
The study also has limitations. Participants were healthy, mostly employed adults recruited in one city, and the results may not apply to people with impaired glucose regulation, older adults or shift workers. One week is short compared with the months or years of short sleep reported in cohort studies, and we cannot say whether the change in fasting glucose would persist, grow or attenuate over a longer period [21]. Participants could not be blinded to their sleep condition, although the outcome was an objective laboratory measure. Diet was recorded rather than controlled, and food records are subject to under-reporting [22]. We measured fasting glucose only; oral glucose tolerance tests or clamp studies would give a fuller picture of glucose regulation after sleep loss.

sections.heading: 4.2 Implications
sections.text: The findings support the inclusion of sleep in advice on the prevention of type 2 diabetes, and suggest that recent sleep may be worth asking about when a borderline fasting glucose result is interpreted [23]. Longer trials, and trials of interventions that extend sleep in habitual short sleepers, are needed to show whether improving sleep lowers glucose over time and whether any benefit is maintained [24, 25].

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: One week of restricted sleep at home raised fasting glucose in healthy adults. Sleep duration should be considered in studies of glucose regulation and in the interpretation of fasting glucose measurements.

Partial retraction: One week of sleep restriction raises fasting glucose: primary and subgroup results

Figure 5 and the associated claims about participants with BMI above 30 are retracted because of a data-merging error that affected that subgroup only. The primary analysis in Table 2 and all other results are unaffected.

draft_doc.title: Sleep, glucose and body weight
draft_doc.authors: Okafor, M.¹, Reyes, J.¹, Tanaka, S.²  ¹ Department of Population Health, Fake Coastal University; ² Centre for Sleep and Circadian Research, Fake Coastal University. Corresponding author: M. Okafor.
draft_doc.abstract: Background: Short sleep is common among adults with overweight and obesity, and both are linked to impaired glucose regulation. Whether lengthening sleep improves glucose control in this group has not been tested in an adequately powered trial. Methods: We describe the design of a randomised controlled trial in which 240 adults with a BMI of 27 or above and habitual sleep of less than six and a half hours a night will be allocated to a six-month sleep extension programme or to general health advice. The primary outcome is fasting plasma glucose at six months. Secondary outcomes include HbA1c, body weight, waist circumference, actigraphic sleep, daytime sleepiness and quality of life. Discussion: The trial will show whether a behavioural programme to lengthen sleep is a feasible and effective addition to lifestyle advice for people at raised risk of type 2 diabetes. Trial registration: to be registered before enrolment.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Type 2 diabetes affects a growing share of adults worldwide, and most new cases arise in people with overweight or obesity [1]. Lifestyle programmes that combine dietary change, increased physical activity and modest weight loss reduce the incidence of diabetes in people at high risk, but their effects in routine practice are smaller than in the original trials, and many participants find the changes hard to sustain over years [2]. There is therefore interest in further, modifiable factors that could be added to existing prevention programmes without making them much more demanding for participants or for the staff who deliver them.
Sleep is one candidate. Population surveys show that a large minority of working adults sleep less than seven hours on work nights, and short sleep is more common among people with obesity than among people of healthy weight, partly because of longer working hours, caring responsibilities, evening screen use and conditions such as sleep apnoea and chronic pain [3]. Short sleep is also socially patterned, being more frequent among people with low income and insecure work, who also carry a higher burden of diabetes.
In prospective cohort studies, short habitual sleep predicts weight gain and incident type 2 diabetes after adjustment for many measured confounders [4]. The associations are consistent across countries and age groups, but residual confounding is hard to exclude, and the direction of the relationship is uncertain: poor metabolic health, depression and pain could themselves shorten sleep. Mendelian randomisation analyses using genetic variants associated with sleep duration have given mixed results, in part because the variants explain little of the variation in sleep [5].
Short sleep may affect body weight and glucose through several pathways. Restricted sleep changes the hormones that regulate appetite, increases the time available for eating, shifts food choice towards energy-dense snacks, and reduces the motivation for physical activity on the following day [7]. It also has direct effects on glucose regulation through the autonomic nervous system, the stress hormone axis and the liver, which do not depend on changes in weight. These pathways suggest that sleep could influence glucose both in the short term and, through weight, in the longer term.
Prevention programmes rarely address sleep. Where sleep is mentioned in current guidance it is usually in general terms, without a specific target or a structured way of helping people to sleep longer, and staff who deliver lifestyle programmes are seldom trained to discuss it [8]. Whether such an addition would be worthwhile depends on evidence that changing sleep changes glucose, which is the gap this trial is designed to fill.
A sleep component would also need to be acceptable to participants. In our consultation with members of the public who had taken part in lifestyle programmes, many described their evenings as the only time available for household tasks, study or rest, and were sceptical of advice simply to go to bed earlier. Several said that they would welcome help in planning their evenings, provided it took account of work and family commitments and did not add to the list of rules they were already asked to follow. These views shaped the design of the programme described below, which is built around personal targets and practical problem solving rather than fixed rules.
The choice of population matters too. People with overweight or obesity who sleep little are at raised risk of diabetes on both counts, are likely to have the most to gain from longer sleep, and are already the main target of prevention programmes. Recruiting from general practice registers, rather than from volunteers who respond to advertisements, should also give a sample closer to the people who would be offered such a programme in routine care.
Experimental studies have mostly asked the opposite question: what happens to metabolism when sleep is shortened in healthy volunteers? Laboratory studies of a few nights of restriction, typically in young men, have shown reduced insulin sensitivity measured by intravenous glucose tolerance tests or clamps, while studies outside the laboratory are fewer and have used shorter or less controlled protocols.
Short sleep acutely raises fasting glucose: one week of restriction raised it by 0.4 mmol/L in healthy adults (Lindqvist and Abara [6]), which motivates our trial.
The converse, that extending sleep in habitual short sleepers improves metabolism, has been tested in only a handful of small trials. A pilot study of sleep extension in short sleepers increased time in bed and reported improvements in self-rated alertness [9], and a trial of sleep hygiene advice in adults with overweight reported a modest increase in sleep duration with no clear change in weight over three months [10]. None of these trials was powered for a glucose outcome, and none recruited people with obesity at raised risk of diabetes specifically.
We have therefore designed a randomised controlled trial to test whether a six-month behavioural programme to lengthen sleep lowers fasting plasma glucose in adults with overweight or obesity who habitually sleep less than six and a half hours a night. This article describes the rationale, design and planned analyses of the trial.

sections.heading: 2.1 Design and setting
sections.text: The trial is a two-arm, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial with blinded outcome assessment, to be conducted in eight general practices and one university clinical research facility. Participants will be followed for six months from randomisation, with outcome visits at baseline, three months and six months. The protocol follows the SPIRIT guidance for trial protocols [12].

sections.heading: 2.2 Participants
sections.text: Adults aged 30 to 65 years with a BMI of 27 kg/m² or above will be identified from practice registers and invited by letter. Eligible participants will report habitual sleep of less than six and a half hours on most work nights, confirmed by seven days of wrist actigraphy at screening, and a wish to sleep longer. We will exclude people with diagnosed diabetes or a screening HbA1c in the diabetic range, people with untreated moderate or severe sleep apnoea on a home sleep test, night and rotating shift workers, people taking hypnotics or other medication that strongly affects sleep or glucose, and people who are pregnant or planning pregnancy. People with a new diagnosis of sleep apnoea at screening will be referred for treatment.

sections.heading: 2.3 Sleep extension programme
sections.text: The intervention combines four individual sessions with a trained health coach over the first eight weeks, delivered face to face or by video, with fortnightly telephone contact for the remainder of the six months. Coaches will help each participant to set a personal target for time in bed, typically an increase of 45 to 60 minutes a night, by moving bedtime earlier rather than wake time later, and to identify and plan around the obstacles that keep them up at night [13]. The sessions draw on techniques used in behavioural treatments for insomnia, including stimulus control, a wind-down routine, and limits on evening light from screens, adapted for people whose problem is insufficient time in bed rather than difficulty falling asleep [14]. Participants will receive a consumer sleep tracker to support self-monitoring, and coaches will review the tracker data with them at each contact.

sections.heading: 2.4 Control condition
sections.text: Participants in the control arm will receive a single session of general health advice covering diet, physical activity and alcohol, with written material, and the same number of telephone contacts as the intervention arm, in which sleep will not be discussed beyond the standard content of the leaflet. They will be offered the sleep extension programme at the end of the trial.

sections.heading: 2.5 Outcomes
sections.text: The primary outcome is fasting plasma glucose at six months, measured after an overnight fast of at least ten hours, in a central laboratory unaware of allocation. Secondary outcomes are HbA1c, fasting insulin, body weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, actigraphic sleep duration and timing over seven days, daytime sleepiness on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, insomnia symptoms, and health-related quality of life [15, 16]. Process measures include attendance at sessions, the fidelity of coaching assessed from recorded sessions, and participants' experience of the programme collected in semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample.

sections.heading: 2.6 Randomisation and blinding
sections.text: Participants will be allocated in a 1:1 ratio by a web-based system after the baseline visit, with minimisation by practice, sex and baseline BMI category. Coaches and participants cannot be blinded to allocation. Research nurses who take outcome measurements, laboratory staff and the trial statistician will be unaware of allocation until the analysis of the primary outcome is complete.

sections.heading: 3. Planned analyses
sections.text: With 120 participants per arm, the trial will have 85% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 to detect a standardised difference of 0.4 in fasting glucose at six months, allowing for 15% loss to follow-up [17]. The primary analysis will compare fasting glucose at six months between arms by intention to treat, in a linear mixed model adjusted for the baseline value and the minimisation factors, with practice as a random effect. Missing outcome data will be handled by multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption, with sensitivity analyses under plausible departures from it [18]. Secondary outcomes will be analysed in the same way. A mediation analysis will examine how much of any effect on glucose is explained by changes in actigraphic sleep and in body weight [19]. Prespecified subgroup analyses by sex and by baseline glucose will be reported with interaction tests and interpreted cautiously. A health economic evaluation will estimate the cost of delivering the programme in primary care.

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
This trial will provide the first adequately powered test of whether lengthening sleep lowers glucose in adults at raised risk of type 2 diabetes. If it does, sleep extension could be added to existing prevention programmes at modest cost, delivered by the same staff who already provide dietary and activity advice.
The effect may be larger in people with obesity, with a doubling reported in participants with BMI above 30 [6, 11].
We have chosen fasting plasma glucose as the primary outcome because it is widely measured in practice, responds within weeks to changes in metabolic state, and is used to define impaired fasting glucose; HbA1c, which reflects glucose over about three months, is a secondary outcome [20]. A six-month follow-up is long enough to capture changes in weight that might follow from longer sleep, but not long enough to show an effect on incident diabetes, which would need a much larger and longer trial.
The main risk to the trial is that participants do not manage to sleep longer. Earlier sleep extension studies achieved increases in time in bed of between half an hour and an hour, but the increase in actual sleep was often smaller, and adherence fell over time [9, 21]. The coaching programme was developed with input from people with short sleep and is designed to be flexible, but the trial includes a process evaluation to understand why it works or fails for different participants. A further risk is that the control condition, by offering general health advice, leads to changes in diet or activity that reduce the difference between arms; we will measure these changes and report them.
The trial also has limits on what it can show. Participants will be people who want to sleep longer, which may make the results more favourable than in a less motivated population. The actigraph and the sleep tracker estimate sleep from movement and may overestimate it in people who lie still while awake [22]. Finally, an effect on glucose would not by itself show which pathway is responsible, although the mediation analysis will give some indication.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: Short sleep is common, modifiable and largely ignored in diabetes prevention. This trial will test whether a practical programme to lengthen sleep improves glucose and related outcomes in adults with overweight or obesity, and will inform whether sleep should become a routine part of lifestyle advice.

sections.heading: Ethics and dissemination
sections.text: The protocol will be submitted to the regional research ethics committee before recruitment begins. Results will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and summarised for participants and participating practices.
